Of, from or relating to Catalonia, Spain.

Catalan.ety: Inherited from Middle English Catalane, from French catalan, from Catalan català. First attested in 1480.

en: Especially or primarily; above all.
Mainly or principally; almost entirely.
Of or relating to a chief.

chiefly.ety: From Middle English chefly; equivalent to chief + -ly (adverbial suffix).

ex.en: Chiefly, I want you to be more frank.
ex.ja: 何よりもまずもっと率直にものを言うようにしてもらいたい。

ex.en: His trouble was chiefly mental.
ex.ja: 彼の病気は主に精神的な物だった。

ex.en: The accident was caused chiefly by the unpredictable weather.
ex.ja: その事故の主な原因は変わりやすい天候であった。

en: The fact or action of giving birth to a child, as the culmination of pregnancy; the process by which it happens.

childbirth.ety: From Middle English childbyrth [and other forms], perhaps a partial calque of Old Norse barnburðr (“childbearing, childbirth”, literally “bairn birth”); equivalent to child + birth. Compare Swedish barnsbörd (“childbirth”), Icelandic barnsburður (“childbirth”).

ex.en: Last time it was a natural childbirth.
ex.ja: 先回は自然分娩でした。

ex.en: Many women pursue higher education and careers, thus delaying marriage and childbirth.
ex.ja: 多くの女性がより高い教養とキャリアを追求し、それ故に結婚と出産を先延ばしにしている。

en: A political philosophy that advocates traditional values.
A risk-averse attitude or approach.

conservatism.ety: Either irregularly from conservative + -ism or from conservate + -ism; ultimately from Latin cōnservāre (“to conserve; to keep, guard, observe”).

note.ja: con（完全に）+ serv（保つ）+ at + ism。そのまま保とうとする考え →「保守主義」。

en: A continuous series or whole, no part of which is noticeably different from its adjacent parts, although the ends or extremes of it are v…
A continuous extent.

continuum.ety: Borrowed from Latin continuum, neuter form of continuus, from contineō (“contain, enclose”).

en: A large, round, pendent chandelier, with spikes around its upper rim to hold candles or lamps, usually hung from the roof of a church.
A region of the skull located along the coronal suture, at the junction between the frontal bone and the two parietal bones.

corona.ety:
The noun is borrowed from Latin corōna (“crown; garland, wreath”), from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē, “type of crown; curved object (door handle, tip of a bow, stern of a ship, etc.)”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). The English word is a doublet of crown, korona, koruna, krona, króna, and krone.
The plural form coronae is borrowed from Latin corōnae.
The verb is derived from the noun.

ex.en: I will not take the Corona vaccine.
ex.ja: コロナワクチンは受けないよ。

A skit or instance of this art or practice.

To costume oneself as (a [usually fictional] character).

en: Showing cowardice; lacking in courage; weakly fearful.

cowardly.ety: From Middle English *cowardly (adjective) and cowardly (adverb), equivalent to coward + -ly. Displaced native Old English earg.

en: To grow plants, notably crops.
To nurture; to foster; to tend.

cultivate.ety: From Medieval Latin cultivātus, perfect passive participle of cultivō (“till, cultivate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from cultīvus (“tilled”), from Latin cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“till, cultivate”), which comes from earlier *quelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”). Cognates include Ancient Greek πέλω (pélō) and Sanskrit चरति (cárati). The same Proto-Indo-European root also gave Latin in-quil-īnus (“inhabitant”) and anculus (“servant”).

ex.en: She cultivated her mind by reading many books.
ex.ja: 彼女は大量の本を読んで精神を陶冶した。

ex.en: Picture books will cultivate the minds of children.
ex.ja: 絵本は子供たちの頭を啓発する。

ex.en: Anyone can cultivate their interest in music.
ex.ja: 誰でも音楽に対する興味を育てる事が出来ます。

note.ja: cult（耕す）+ iv + ate。耕す →「栽培する・（能力を）養う・（関係を）築く」。

en: To challenge (someone) or brave (a hazard or opposition).
To refuse to obey.

defy.ety: From Old French desfier, from Vulgar Latin *disfidare (“renounce one's faith”), from Latin dis- (“away”) + fidus (“faithful”). Meaning shifted in the 14th century from "be disloyal" to "challenge". Contrast confide, fidelity, faith.

ex.en: I defy you to make it public.
ex.ja: できるというならそれを表沙汰にするがよい。

ex.en: I defy you to solve this problem.
ex.ja: この問題が解けるならやってみろ。

ex.en: They defied the laws of the king.
ex.ja: 彼らは王様の作った法律に反抗した。

en: The state of being unequal; difference.
Incongruity.

disparity.ety: From Middle French disparité, from Latin disparitātem, accusative of disparitās, from dispār + -tās, from dis- + pār. By surface analysis, dis- + parity.

note.ja: dis（否定）+ par（等しい）+ ity。等しくないこと →「格差・不均衡」。

en: Any female celebrity, usually a well known singer or actress.

diva.ety: From Italian diva (“diva, goddess”), from Latin dīva (“goddess”), female of dīvus (“divine, divine one; notably a deified mortal”), from Old Latin deivā, from Proto-Italic *deiwā (“goddess”), feminine of *deiwos (“god”), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós (“god”).

ex.en: Mary was known as Diva of the Century.
ex.ja: メアリーは世紀の歌姫と呼ばれていた。

ex.en: Mary was called the diva of the century.
ex.ja: メアリーは世紀の歌姫と呼ばれていた。

ex.en: Mary was referred to as the diva of the century.
ex.ja: メアリーは世紀の歌姫と呼ばれていた。

en: To turn aside from a course.
To distract.

divert.ety: From Middle English diverten, Old French divertir (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin di- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

ex.en: The audience was diverted with funny stories.
ex.ja: 聴衆はおかしい話で楽しんだ。

ex.en: He diverted himself by listening to music.
ex.ja: 彼は音楽を聴いて気を紛らした。

ex.en: They diverted the river to supply water somewhere else.
ex.ja: 彼らは他のところへ水を供給するために川の流れの向きを変えた。

note.ja: di（離れて）+ vert（向ける）。別の方へ向ける →「そらす・転用する・気晴らしさせる」。

en: Grace, refinement, and beauty in movement, appearance, or manners.
Restraint and grace of style.

elegance.ety: From Middle French élégance, from Latin ēlegantia (“exquisiteness; refinement, elegance”).

ex.en: Everybody at the party was charmed by her elegance.
ex.ja: パーティーにいた人は誰もかも彼女の優雅さに魅せられた。

ex.en: This is a house that exudes an air of elegance.
ex.ja: これは上品な佇まいを漂わせた家だ。

en: The face of a building, especially the front view or elevation.
The face or front (most visible side) of any other thing, such as the prospect of an organ.

facade.ety: Borrowed from French façade, from Italian facciata, a derivation of faccia (“front”), from Latin faciēs (“face”); compare face.

note.ja: イタリア語 facciata（顔のような正面）から。fac（顔）。建物の顔 →「（建物の）正面・見せかけ」。

en: A farmer's residence.
A house that was once a farmer's residence albeit today lived in by residents whose occupation is not farming.

ex.en: He lives in a farmhouse remote from the world.
ex.ja: 彼は人里離れた農家に住んでいる。

ex.en: They walked with him to an old wooden building near the farmhouse.
ex.ja: 少年達はウッドさんについて、農家の近くにある古い木造の建物へ歩いて行きました。

ex.en: Tony and his mother arrived at the farmhouse and walked through the farmyard.
ex.ja: トニーと母親はその農家に着き、農家の庭を歩いて行きました。

en: A small, wingless, parasitic insect of the order Siphonaptera, renowned for its bloodsucking habits and jumping abilities.
To remove fleas from (an animal).

flea.ety:
From Middle English fle, from Old English flēah, flēa, from Proto-West Germanic *flauh, from Proto-Germanic *flauhaz (compare West Frisian flie, Low German Flo, Flö, Dutch vlo, German Floh, Icelandic fló), from pre-Germanic *plóukos, *plówkos, from or akin to Proto-Indo-European *plus- (compare Latin pulex, Sanskrit प्लुषि (plúṣi)).
The archaic plural fleen is from Middle English fleen, flen, from Old English flēan (“fleas”).

ex.en: Let's go to the flea market tomorrow.
ex.ja: 明日フリーマーケットに行こうよ！

ex.en: I gave my old clothes for the flea market sale.
ex.ja: 私は自分の古着をのみの市セールに寄付した。

ex.en: Is there anywhere I can go to find a flea market?
ex.ja: フリーマーケットをやっている場所がありますか。

en: A small bag used chiefly by women for carrying various small personal items, sometimes considered as a fashion accessory.
To attack verbally or subject to criticism (typically used of a woman).

handbag.ety: From hand + bag. The music genre is named from women dancing around a pile of their handbags in nightclubs. The verb is a reference to Margaret Thatcher's handbag.

ex.en: Mary got her phone out of her handbag.
ex.ja: メアリーはバッグから携帯を取り出した。

ex.en: She felt in her handbag for her ring.

en: Very fine solid particles (smoke, dust) or liquid droplets (moisture) suspended in the air, slightly limiting visibility. (Compare fog, m…
A reduction of transparency of a clear gas or liquid.
To be or become hazy, or thick with haze.

haze.ety:
* The earliest instances are of the latter part of the 17th century.
* Possibly back-formation from hazy.
* Compare Old Norse höss (“grey”), akin to Old English hasu (“gray”).

ex.en: My mind was in a haze after drinking so much.
ex.ja: 私は飲みすぎて頭がもうろうとしていた。

ex.en: My name is Hase.
ex.ja: 私のお名前はハセです。

ex.en: The haze enveloped London.
ex.ja: もやがロンドンの町をすっぽりと包んだ。

Inherited from Middle English hemp, from Old English henep, from Proto-West Germanic *hanapi, from Proto-Germanic *hanapiz. Doublet of cannabis and canvas.

en: A sudden pull.
Any of various knots used to attach a rope to an object other than another rope.
To pull with a jerk.
To attach, tie or fasten.

hitch.ety: Probably from Middle English hicchen, hytchen, icchen (“to move; to move as with a jerk”), of obscure origin. Lacks cognates in other languages. Compare itch, hike.

ex.en: Janet and Bill are going to get hitched in June.
ex.ja: ジャネットとビルは６月に結婚する。

en: An incarnate being or form.
A version or iteration (of something).

incarnation.ety: From Middle English incarnacion, borrowed from Old French incarnacion, from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin incarnatio, from Late Latin incarnari (“to be made flesh”).

en: The forcible inclusion or entry of an external group or individual; the act of intruding.
A penetration by hackers, a computer virus, etc.

intrusion.ety: From Middle English intrusioun, from Old French intrusion, from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from intrūdō, from Latin in- + trūdō.

ex.en: Sorry for the intrusion.
ex.ja: お邪魔してしまってすみません。

en: Opposite in effect, nature or order.
Reverse, opposite in order.
An inverted state: a state in which something has been turned (properly) upside down or (loosely) inside out or backwards.
The reverse of any procedure or process.
To compute the bearing and distance between two points.

inverse.ety: Recorded since 1440, from Latin inversus, the past participle of invertere (“to invert”), itself from in- (“against, in”) + vertere (“to turn”).

note.ja: in（反対に）+ vers（向ける）+ e。向きを反対にした →「逆の・反対の」。

en: Having the order or direction exchanged; for example, turned upside down, reversed, or in any other way opposite or contrary and swapped.
Having the lowest note transposed an octave higher.

ex.en: Through the lens the image was inverted.
ex.ja: レンズを通ると像は逆になった。

ex.en: Place your skis in an inverted V.
ex.ja: あなたのスキーを逆Ｖ字型にしなさい。

en: The act of irritating or annoying.
The state of being irritated.

irritation.ety: Borrowed from Middle French irritation, from Latin irrītātiō, from irrītāre (“to excite”). By surface analysis, irritate + -ion.

ex.en: There was no irritation on his part.
ex.ja: 彼としては少しもいらいらしてなかった。

ex.en: Her mood graduated to irritation.
ex.ja: 彼女の気分は次第にいら立ちはじめた。

en: Any word used as the key to a code.
Any word used in a reference work to link to other words or other information.
To tag with keywords, as for example to facilitate searching.
Expending or bestowing profusely; profuse; prodigal.
Superabundant; excessive.
To give out extremely generously; to squander.
To give out to (somebody) extremely generously.

lavish.ety: From Middle English laves, lavas, lavage (“extravagant, wasteful, prodigal”), from lavas (“excessive abundance”), from Old French lavasse, lavache (“torrent of rain”); possibly later conflated in some senses by Middle English laven (“to pour out”), equivalent to lave + -ish. Compare Scots lawage, lavisch, lavish (“unrestrained, excessively prodigal, extravagant”). Compare also English lavy (“lavish, liberal”), Dutch lafenis (“lavishness”).

ex.en: He is lavish with his money.
ex.ja: 彼は金を惜しみなく使う。

ex.en: He's lavish with his money.
ex.ja: 彼は金を惜しみなく使う。

ex.en: The real estate broker was lavish in his spending in Ginza.
ex.ja: その不動産屋は銀座で気前よく金を使った。

en: A means of providing the necessities of life for oneself (for example, a job or income).

livelihood.ety: From Middle English liflode, from Old English līflād (“course of life, conduct”), from līf (“life”) + lād (“course, journey”), later altered under the influence of lively, -hood. Compare life, lode.

ex.en: Life and livelihood are the same thing.
ex.ja: 金と命は同義語だよ。

ex.en: How is livelihood in America these day?
ex.ja: 最近のアメリカ人の暮らし振りはどうですか。

ex.en: The ordinary people had their livelihood in farming rice.
ex.ja: 庶民のなりわいは、米をつくることだった。

en: A small falcon, Falco columbarius, that breeds in northern North America, Europe, and Asia.

merlin.ety: From Middle English merlioun, merlion, marlyon, merlyon, merlinge, from Old French emerillon, esmerillon, from Old Frankish *smiril (“falcon, hawk”), from Proto-Germanic *smirilaz (“falcon, merlin”). Cognate with Old High German smirl (“falcon”), Old Norse smyrill (“falcon”).

en: Consisting of a variety of ingredients or parts.
Having diverse characteristics, abilities or appearances.

miscellaneous.ety: Borrowed from Latin miscellāneus, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“mix”).

ex.en: I keep all my miscellaneous files in this folder.
ex.ja: このフォルダーに、「その他」に分類される全てのファイルを入れて保管しています。

ex.en: That drawer is full of miscellaneous items.
ex.ja: あの引き出しの中は雑多なもので溢れかえっている。

en: An assemblage or display; a gathering, collection of people or things.
An assembling or review of troops, as for parade, verification of numbers, inspection, exercise, or introduction into service.
To be gathered together for parade, inspection, exercise, or the like (especially of a military force); to come together as parts of a fo…
To collect, call or assemble together, such as troops or a group for inspection, orders, display etc.

muster.ety: From Middle English musteren, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mostrer, Middle French monstrer, moustrer (whence the noun monstre, which gave the English noun), from Latin mōnstrō (“to show”), from moneō (“to admonish”). Cognate with French montrer (“to show”), Italian mostrare (“to show”), Spanish mostrar (“to show”). See also monster.

ex.en: I mustered up my courage and went there.
ex.ja: 私は思い切ってそこに行った。

ex.en: I'm sure it'll work out, so muster your courage!
ex.ja: きっとうまく行くから、勇気を出せ！

ex.en: She finally mustered up the courage to ask him for more money.
ex.ja: 彼女はついに勇気を出して彼の借金の申し込みをした。

en: A string or flat strip of pasta or other dough, usually cooked (at least initially) by boiling, and served in soup or in a dry form mixed…
An object which is long and thin like a noodle (sense 1).
To hum or sing (a tune) at a low pitch or volume.

noodle.ety:
Borrowed from Dutch noedel (“noodle”), or from its etymon German Nudel (“piece of pasta, noodle”); further etymology uncertain, probably a variant of Knödel (“dumpling”), from Middle High German knödel (“dumpling; small knot”), and then either:
* from knode, knote (“knot”) (from Old High German knodo, knoto (“knot”), perhaps ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *knappō (“knob; boy”)) + -el (diminutive suffix); or
* from Ladin menùdli (“small dough dumpling in soup”), probably from Latin minutulus (“very small, tiny”) (in the sense of food chopped into small pieces), a diminutive of minūtu

ex.en: You're right. The noodle broth here is a bit expensive.
ex.ja: その通りさ。ここの麺の出汁はちょっと値が張るんだ。

en: Originally, the DuPont company trade name for polyamide, a copolymer whose molecules consist of alternating diamine and dicarboxylic acid…
A stocking originally fabricated from nylon; also used generically for any long, sheer stocking worn on a woman's legs.

nylon.ety: Coined by the company DuPont in 1938. According to the company, the name was formed from the random generic syllable nyl- + the common fiber suffix -on (as in rayon and Dacron), said to be ultimately from cotton.

ex.en: These nylon socks wash well.
ex.ja: このナイロンソックスは、洗濯がきく。

ex.en: Nylon stockings often run.
ex.ja: ナイロンストッキングはすぐ伝線する。

en: To ride across or beyond something.
To ride over the top of something, usually forcibly.
A mechanism, device or procedure used to counteract an automatic control.
A royalty.

override.ety: From Middle English overriden, from Old English oferrīdan, equivalent to over- + ride. Cognate with Dutch overrijden, German überreiten, Danish override.

ex.en: The President vetoed the bill, but Congress overrode his veto.
ex.ja: 大統領はその法案に対して拒否権を行使しましたが、議会が再度それを無効にしました。

ex.en: Under the Constitution, the lower chamber's resolutions override those of the upper chamber.
ex.ja: 憲法の規定に従い衆院の議決が参院に優越する。

en: An allotrope of oxygen (symbol O₃) having three atoms in the molecule instead of the usual two; it is a toxic gas, generated from oxygen …
Fresh air, especially that breathed at the seaside and smelling of seaweed.
To treat with ozone.

ozone.ety:
From German Ozon, coined 1840 by Christian Friedrich Schönbein, from Ancient Greek ὄζον (ózon), neuter participle of ὄζω (ózō, “I smell”), in reference to its pungent odour.
The “fresh air” sense is from an erroneous former belief that seaweed contains and releases ozone.

ex.en: Without the ozone layer, we would be in danger.
